items.stem: A single, unredundant server reports 99.97% availability over the last quarter, purely by luck — it never happened to be hit by an outage window. A separate service is built with redundant instances across two zones and automatic failover, but had a rough month and only measured 99.5%. Which statement correctly separates what each number shows from what each design achieves?

options.text: The first figure is a measured result that can exist without any high-availability design behind it; the second is a high-availability design that can still miss its own target after a bad month.
options.why: Availability is an observed quantity; high availability is an architecture. Either can occur without the other, in both directions.

options.text: The unredundant server must be the more highly available of the two, since its measured number is larger.
options.why: This treats the measured percentage as if it proved the underlying design, conflating the metric with the architecture that is supposed to raise it.

options.text: Both figures describe the same property, so the two services are equally reliable regardless of design.
options.why: Reliability properties such as fault tolerance are separate from an availability figure and are not implied by it.

options.text: A redundant, automatically-failing-over design is guaranteed to score higher than an unredundant one over any measurement window — treating the design as a promise about the outcome of any single window, rather than about the long-run average it is actually meant to shift.
options.why: High availability lowers the chance of a bad month; it does not guarantee the outcome of any single measured window, as this scenario shows.

items.rationale: Availability is what you measure over a window; high availability is what you build to raise it. The comparison block's whole point is that a number is not an architecture — each can occur without the other, as this scenario deliberately shows in both directions.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against the Reliability Pillar availability page, which defines availability as "the percentage of time that a workload is available for use", calculated over a period such as a month — an observed quantity — and separately shows that independent redundant components raise the theoretical availability, i.e. a design choice. So a measured figure can exist with no redundancy behind it and a redundant design can still measure badly over one window. No distractor is also correct: o2 infers architecture from a single measured number, which the page's own definition does not license; o3 asserts the two figures describe the same property, contradicting the measured-versus-designed split; o4 claims a guarantee for any single window, whereas the page's calculation is of theoretical availability over a period, not of any individual month's outcome. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: An SRE team is choosing between two internal SLO targets, both measured over a 30-day month: 99.95% and 99.9%. Relaxing the target from 99.95% to 99.9% permits how much additional downtime across the month?

options.text: About 21.6 more minutes; the allowance grows from roughly 21.6 minutes to roughly 43.2 minutes.
options.why: 43.2 minus 21.6 minutes is 21.6 minutes; both figures follow from (1 minus availability) times the 30-day window.

options.text: About 4.3 more minutes, since relaxing by one nine only ever changes the figure by the smallest listed increment.
options.why: This mistakes 99.95% to 99.9% for a change of one full nine; the ten-times step applies between whole nines, not half-nines, and understates the real difference.

options.text: About 7.2 hours more, matching the jump from three nines down to two nines rather than the half-step asked about.
options.why: That figure is the monthly allowance recovered going from 99.9% down to 99%, a full nine away from the pair in the question.

options.text: No measurable difference, because both targets round to the same permitted downtime once expressed per month.
options.why: The two monthly allowances differ by a factor of two, which is not a rounding artefact.

items.rationale: Monthly downtime allowance is (1 minus availability) times 30 days times 24 times 60 minutes: about 43.2 minutes at 99.9% and about 21.6 minutes at 99.95%, a difference of 21.6 minutes recomputed directly from the definition rather than copied from the guide's table.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the arithmetic was cited to Chapter 4 of the SRE book, which discusses SLO targets but carries no downtime table. Appendix A of the same book tabulates it directly: 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes and 99.95% allows 21.6 minutes per 30 days, so the difference is 21.6 minutes — the key, now cited to the table that states it. Recomputed independently: (1 - 0.999) x 43,200 minutes = 43.2, (1 - 0.9995) x 43,200 = 21.6. No distractor is also correct: 4.3 minutes matches no pair in the table; 7.2 hours is the 99.9%-to-99% step (the table gives 21.6 hours per 30 days at 99%, and 21.6 h - 43.2 min is about 20.9 h, so even that figure is not 7.2 h — o3's why correctly identifies it as a full-nine step away and it is wrong either way); and o4's "no measurable difference" is refuted by a factor-of-two gap. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A design keeps two application servers on independent power feeds in separate racks, but nothing watches them and nothing redirects traffic if one goes down. Is the arrangement highly available?

options.text: No. Redundancy is only one of the two required ingredients; nothing detects a failure or moves traffic away from it.
options.why: High availability needs redundancy plus automatic failover; a spare with no mechanism to use it is not yet either.

options.text: Yes — duplicate hardware placed in separate failure domains is what the term names.
options.why: That describes redundancy, the ingredient supplying spare capacity, not the completed design that also needs automatic failover.

options.text: Yes, provided the two servers are also stateless, since statelessness is what makes availability possible.
options.why: Statelessness is the precondition for scaling instances interchangeably; it does not supply the missing detection-and-redirect mechanism here.

options.text: No, and no amount of automatic failover fixes it either, because true high availability requires zero user-visible interruption.
options.why: Zero interruption is the stricter fault-tolerance bar; high availability accepts a brief detection-and-switch window, which failover would supply here.

items.rationale: High availability requires both redundancy and automatic failover. This design has only the first ingredient — duplicate components with no health check and no redirection — so it is not yet highly available, though adding failover would complete it.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL11-BP02, which frames failing over as requiring systems in place to move to healthy resources and names detection as a design decision, and against the RDS Multi-AZ page, where high availability is delivered by a standby in another Availability Zone plus an automatic failover action — redundancy plus a mechanism that uses it. Two racked servers with nothing watching them supply only the first half. No distractor is also correct: o2 names redundancy alone, which is the ingredient not the design; o3 makes statelessness sufficient, and neither source treats statelessness as a detection-and-redirect mechanism; o4 asserts zero interruption is required for high availability, which the RDS page contradicts by calling a deployment with a failover event highly available. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A cloud provider's contract promises 99.99% monthly availability with service credits if missed. A customer runs a single instance in a single zone on that platform. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The provider's figure is a contractual promise about the platform; the customer's own architecture, not the contract, determines whether their service is actually highly available.
options.why: An SLA prices the provider's own shortfall; it says nothing about what an unredundant deployment built on top of it will achieve.

options.text: The customer's service inherits 99.99% availability automatically, since that is what the SLA guarantees them — a substitution that ignores everything the customer’s own architecture would have to contribute for that number to hold.
options.why: This is the substitution the SLA comparison warns against: a high provider SLA does not make an unredundant single-zone deployment highly available.

options.text: The SLA is itself a design for high availability, since it specifies redundancy and failover requirements.
options.why: An SLA is a contract with a remedy, not an architecture; it names no redundancy or failover mechanism at all.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because SLA figures are never comparable to a customer's own measured availability.
options.why: Both are availability percentages over a window, which makes them directly comparable; the issue is what produced each one, not their comparability.

items.rationale: A high provider SLA is a promise about the platform's own shortfall risk. A customer who deploys a single instance in a single zone has built no redundancy or failover of their own, so their service's availability is set by their architecture, not by the number in the contract.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL11-BP07, which states that if you publish or privately agree an availability target or uptime SLA you must verify your architecture and operational processes are designed to support it, and that a workload should weigh its dependencies' own SLAs — exactly the split between a contractual promise and what a customer's own single-zone architecture achieves. No distractor is also correct: o2's inheritance claim is what BP07 exists to deny; o3 calls an SLA an architecture, and neither the SLA best practice nor the availability page treats a contract as specifying redundancy or failover; o4 denies comparability, but the availability page defines a single percentage-over-a-period metric that both figures are instances of. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: Two systems each survive a single-node failure. In the first, users see a short window of errors while a health check detects the failure and traffic is redirected to a standby. In the second, redundant nodes are already running the same work concurrently, so nothing is switched and no error appears anywhere. Which is fault tolerant, and why?

options.text: The second. Fault tolerance means no user-visible interruption at all, because the redundant capacity was already doing the work rather than waiting to be switched to.
options.why: The absence of any interruption, not merely a fast one, is the property that separates fault tolerance from high availability.

options.text: The first, because detecting a failure and redirecting traffic is the textbook definition of tolerating a fault — collapsing the whole distinction the comparison exists to preserve between a brief switch and no interruption at all.
options.why: Detect-then-redirect is exactly the high-availability mechanism, and it is the brief interruption during that process that fault tolerance is defined against.

options.text: Both equally, since either arrangement keeps the service running after one node is lost.
options.why: Both keep the service running, but the comparison turns on whether the user notices anything, and only one arrangement guarantees they do not.

options.text: Neither, because a genuinely fault-tolerant system would also survive the loss of every replica at once.
options.why: Fault tolerance covers a defined class of faults, not every conceivable failure; a correlated loss of all replicas falling outside that class does not disqualify the label.

items.rationale: Fault tolerance is defined by the absence of interruption: concurrent redundant capacity absorbs the fault with nothing to switch, whereas high availability accepts a brief detection-and-failover window. The comparison block's separating axis is exactly this interruption, not whether the service ultimately survives.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against the NIST CSRC glossary, which defines fault tolerance as "a property of a system that allows proper operation even if components fail" — proper operation continuing through the failure, not resuming after a switch — read against the RDS Multi-AZ page, where high availability is delivered by a failover event to a standby, i.e. a switch with a window. The second system, with redundant nodes already doing the work, is the fault-tolerant one. No distractor is also correct: o2 names detect-then-redirect, which is the failover path both AWS pages describe, not proper operation through the fault; o3 makes survival alone sufficient, which erases the interruption axis; o4 demands survival of every conceivable failure, which "even if components fail" does not require. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A quorum-based data store is marketed as fault tolerant because it keeps serving reads and writes as long as a majority of its members are reachable. A network partition then isolates every member from every other at once. What does 'fault tolerant' fail to promise here?

options.text: Nothing beyond the defined fault class, given that a fault-tolerant system survives the failures it was designed for, and a total partition of every member falls outside that class.
options.why: The definition is bounded: it guarantees continued correct operation for a stated class of faults, not immunity from every possible one.

options.text: It fails to promise anything, since a properly fault-tolerant system is, by definition, 100% available.
options.why: Treating fault tolerant as a synonym for always available is the specific error this concept is examined on; 100% availability is not an achievable target for any real service.

options.text: It fails to promise a fast recovery, since fault-tolerant systems are only rated on how quickly they detect and fail over — a claim that quietly assumes every fault-tolerant design is also the fastest-recovering one, which the definition never promises.
options.why: Detection and failover describe high availability's recovery path; a fault-tolerant design has no switch to time in the first place.

options.text: It fails to promise redundancy, since quorum systems can operate with only a single reachable member.
options.why: Quorum systems require a majority of members, which presupposes redundancy; the gap here is about fault class, not about whether redundancy exists.

items.rationale: Fault tolerance is a property against a defined class of faults. A quorum design tolerates the loss of a minority of members, but a partition that isolates every member simultaneously is a correlated failure outside that class, and the system is not obligated to survive it.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against the NIST glossary definition, which is bounded by construction: proper operation "even if components fail" is a promise about component failures the design covers, not about a partition isolating every member at once. No distractor is also correct: o2 equates fault tolerance with 100% availability, which the definition never states and which the Reliability Pillar availability page contradicts by treating availability as a target below 100%; o3 rates fault tolerance on detection and failover speed, which is the failover path, not proper operation through the fault; o4 claims quorum systems can run on a single member, which contradicts the majority requirement stated in the stem. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A team says 'we run two application servers, so we have redundancy.' What has not yet been established about the pair?

options.text: Whether they sit in independent failure domains (separate hosts, racks or zones), so the event that takes out one cannot also take out the other.
options.why: Redundancy only survives failure if the duplicate is placed somewhere the same fault cannot reach both copies.

options.text: Whether the servers are running the newest version of the operating system — a detail that says nothing about whether the two machines could both be lost to the same rack, power feed or zone-level event.
options.why: Patch currency is a maintenance concern unrelated to whether the pair can survive a shared failure.

options.text: Whether the pair has been load tested at its maximum request rate.
options.why: Capacity testing measures throughput, not whether the two servers share a single point of failure.

options.text: Whether the servers are billed on a monthly or an annual commitment.
options.why: Billing terms have no bearing on whether the pair is placed in independent failure domains.

items.rationale: Redundancy is duplication placed so that one failure is survivable, which depends on the duplicates sharing no single failure domain. Two servers in the same rack on the same power feed are not redundant against a rack- or feed-level failure even though there are two of them.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL10-BP01, which instructs distributing workload data and resources across multiple Availability Zones or Regions and states that a fundamental principle is to avoid single points of failure "including the underlying physical infrastructure" — so what is unestablished about two servers is whether the same physical event can take both. No distractor is also correct: patch currency (o2), load-test results (o3) and billing terms (o4) are each independently true statements about unrelated properties, and none of them bears on shared failure domains. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A service is provisioned N+1: three units of load require four running instances. One instance is taken down for planned maintenance. What is true of the remaining capacity?

options.text: Full load can still be carried on the three instances that remain, which is exactly what the extra unit was provisioned for.
options.why: N+1 means one more unit than load requires, so losing any single unit — planned or not — still leaves enough capacity.

options.text: The service is now under-provisioned, since N+1 only covers a single simultaneous unplanned failure, not planned maintenance.
options.why: N+1 is agnostic to why a unit is unavailable; the spare capacity covers the loss of any one unit regardless of cause.

options.text: Traffic must be rejected until the instance returns, because active-passive redundancy requires a promotion step first.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario states the units are active-passive; N+1 sizing is commonly used with active-active capacity that needs no promotion.

options.text: The remaining instances must each individually double their capacity to absorb the loss.
options.why: N+1 sizing already accounts for one unit's worth of spare capacity spread across the pool; no individual instance needs to be resized.

items.rationale: N+1 provisions one more unit than the load strictly requires, so the loss of any single unit — whether by failure or by planned maintenance — still leaves enough capacity to carry the full load on the survivors.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL11-BP05, which states that the capacity needed after losing a zone must already have been provisioned before the failure so the workload operates in a single mode — spare capacity provisioned ahead of the loss is exactly what N+1 sizing buys, and the source draws no distinction between a planned and an unplanned reason for the unit being gone. No distractor is also correct: o2 makes N+1 conditional on the cause of the loss, which nothing in the static-stability guidance supports; o3 assumes active-passive, which the stem never states; o4 demands each survivor double its capacity, which contradicts one unit of spare capacity being enough. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A backend fails its health check and a load balancer simply stops sending it traffic; the rest of the pool absorbs the load and nothing else changes. A separate incident has the primary database die outright, and a DNS record is switched to point at a standby that then serves all writes. Which of the two events is failover?

options.text: Only the database incident — the whole workload moved to a standby, which is what failover names; the load balancer event removed one member from a pool that keeps working the same way.
options.why: Failover switches the service as a whole onto a standby when the active component fails; routing around one dead backend in an otherwise-unchanged pool is ordinary load balancing.

options.text: Both — a health check stopping traffic to a dead backend is exactly the same event as switching a whole service to a standby — erasing the distinction the whole comparison exists to draw, between removing one member from a pool and switching the entire service.
options.why: The two overlap only in that both react to a health check; one removes a single member from a working pool and the other switches the entire service, which is not the same event.

options.text: Only the load balancer event, since load balancing runs continuously and is therefore the more resilient of the two mechanisms.
options.why: Running continuously describes load balancing's normal-path behaviour; it does not make the health-check removal a case of failover, which is defined by the whole-service switch.

options.text: Neither, because both are examples of auto-scaling responding to reduced capacity.
options.why: Neither event adds or removes instances against a metric or schedule, which is what auto-scaling does; both concern routing around or replacing a failed component.

items.rationale: Failover is the exception path: the whole workload moves to a standby only when the active component fails. Load balancing is the normal path, acting on every request; a health check pulling one dead member from an otherwise-healthy pool is not the same event as switching the service.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL11-BP02, which describes failover as moving to healthy resources in unimpaired locations — promoting a replica and then pointing traffic at the new endpoint, a whole-service switch — read against the ELB overview, where health checks mean "the load balancer sends requests only to the healthy ones", which is the normal request path continuing unchanged. No distractor is also correct: o2 equates the two events, which the sources separate; o3 calls continuous operation a reason to name the pool event failover, which does not follow; o4 calls both auto-scaling, and neither adds nor removes capacity against a metric. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A DNS-based failover promotes a standby within thirty seconds of the primary failing, but clients keep sending requests to the dead address for several more minutes. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Cached DNS records; resolvers and clients keep using the old address until the record's time-to-live expires.
options.why: A long TTL can dominate the total outage even when detection and the record switch were both fast.

options.text: The failure threshold was set too low, so the health check never actually declared the primary unhealthy.
options.why: The scenario states the standby was promoted within thirty seconds, meaning the health check did fire; the delay is happening after that point.

options.text: The standby has not finished failback yet, so it is refusing the redirected connections.
options.why: Failback is the later, separate step of returning to a recovered primary; nothing in the scenario describes the standby refusing traffic.

options.text: Load balancing rules on the standby are still routing requests back to the primary by mistake.
options.why: Load balancing distributes traffic across a pool of live backends; it does not explain clients resolving a name to the address of a component that is already down.

items.rationale: Failover's total delay is the sum of several configured values: probe interval times failure threshold, plus the time for the redirection to take effect. With DNS-based failover, a cached record means clients keep using the old address until the TTL expires, regardless of how fast detection and promotion were.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item turns on DNS record caching, and the Route 53 welcome page it cited covers domain registration, DNS routing and health checking without ever mentioning TTL or resolver caching. The Route 53 record-values page states it directly: TTL is the time "that you want DNS recursive resolvers to cache information about this record", and with a longer value "it takes longer for changes to the record (for example, a new IP address) to take effect" because "recursive resolvers use the values in their cache for longer periods" — which is the key. No distractor is also correct: o2 contradicts the stem, which says promotion happened within thirty seconds; o3 invokes failback, a later return to the recovered primary that the stem does not describe; o4 blames load-balancing rules, which do not govern what address a client's resolver returns. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A platform can be given more servers by hand whenever traffic grows, and someone remembers to remove them again once traffic falls. Is the platform elastic?

options.text: No, because elasticity means capacity provisioned and released rapidly and in step with demand, which a cycle waiting on someone to remember is not.
options.why: Elasticity is scalability plus two things: automation, and capacity being released again as demand falls.

options.text: Yes, because capacity is eventually returned to its original level once demand drops — mistaking the eventual return of capacity for the automatic, no-human-involved behaviour the definition actually requires.
options.why: NIST defines rapid elasticity as capabilities "elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand"; capacity that comes back whenever a person next remembers is neither rapid nor commensurate with demand.

options.text: Yes, since the platform can clearly be given more resources and make use of them.
options.why: Being able to grow with more resources is the definition of scalability, which elasticity implies but is not itself sufficient for.

options.text: No, because the platform has no defined upper bound on how many servers can be added.
options.why: An unbounded ceiling is a property of horizontal scaling's headroom, not the reason this platform falls short of elastic.

items.rationale: Elasticity adds automation and bidirectionality on top of scalability: capacity must be provisioned and released without a human deciding each time. A platform that only scales when someone remembers to act on it both ways is scalable, not elastic.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the distractor rationale: o2's why asserted that "NIST ties elasticity to capacities provisioned and released automatically", but SP 800-145 s2 actually reads "capabilities can be elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand" — the hedge "in some cases" makes automation typical rather than definitional, so the why overstated the source. The why now quotes NIST verbatim and rests on the two conditions NIST does state without hedge: rapid, and commensurate with demand. The key was rewritten to turn on the same two conditions rather than on automation alone, and still holds: a cycle that moves only when a person remembers is neither rapid nor tracking demand. No distractor is also correct: o2's "eventually returned" fails the rapid/commensurate test; o3 describes scalability, which NIST's on-demand self-service and elasticity characteristics treat as the weaker property; o4's unbounded-ceiling reason is not why the platform falls short. Each why now states a true fact.

items.stem: An e-commerce platform automatically adds instances during a flash sale and automatically removes them again once demand returns to normal. Which of the two compared terms best names this behaviour, and what would be lost if only the removal step were dropped?

options.text: Elasticity; dropping the automatic removal would leave only scalability, since capacity would grow but never shrink back.
options.why: Automatic and bidirectional is exactly elasticity's definition; removing the shrink-back half leaves only the ability to grow.

options.text: Scalability — and dropping the removal step would make no difference, since scalability never required shrinking in the first place.
options.why: The behaviour described — automatic in both directions — is elasticity's definition, not merely scalability's, so this undercounts what is actually being described.

options.text: Elasticity — and dropping the removal step would remove the platform's ability to add capacity at all.
options.why: Removing the shrink-back half leaves the grow half intact; the platform would still add instances during the sale, just never release them afterwards.

options.text: High availability — and dropping the removal step would create a single point of failure.
options.why: High availability concerns surviving component failure, not capacity tracking demand; nothing here is about a single point of failure.

items.rationale: Automatic growth and automatic shrink-back together are elasticity; NIST names this rapid elasticity as one of cloud computing's essential characteristics. Removing only the shrink-back half leaves a system that scales out under load and never scales back in — expensive, not elastic.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against SP 800-145 s2, which lists rapid elasticity as an essential characteristic — capabilities provisioned and released to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand — and against the EC2 Auto Scaling page, where scaling policies "launch or terminate instances as demand on your application increases or decreases": adding for the sale and removing afterwards is the outward-and-inward pair, and dropping the inward half leaves growth only. No distractor is also correct: o2 names scalability for behaviour NIST describes as elasticity; o3 claims the shrink-back removes the ability to add, which does not follow; o4 names high availability, which concerns component failure and not demand tracking. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A single-writer relational database is running out of capacity on its write path, and the write path cannot be split across multiple nodes. Which capacity move fits, and what does it cost?

options.text: Vertical scaling — moving the database to a larger instance type — at the cost of a restart and a hard ceiling once the largest available machine is reached.
options.why: A workload that cannot be divided is exactly the case vertical scaling answers, and its two limits are the restart and the ceiling.

options.text: Horizontal scaling — adding more database nodes behind a load balancer — since that removes the single point of failure with no interruption cost.
options.why: The scenario states the write path cannot be split; adding nodes behind a load balancer does nothing for work that is not distributable.

options.text: Auto-scaling — letting a scaling group add database instances against a CPU metric.
options.why: Auto-scaling automates adding and removing instances of a distributable workload; it does not apply to a single-writer path that cannot be spread across instances.

options.text: Caching the write path's results so fewer writes reach the database directly.
options.why: Caching serves repeated reads from a stored copy; it has no mechanism for absorbing writes, which must still reach the authoritative store.

items.rationale: A single-writer path with no way to divide the work is the textbook case for vertical scaling: resize to a bigger instance, at the cost of a restart, and accept that the move is finished once the largest instance type is reached.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: both vertical-scaling items cited the EC2 Auto Scaling page, which is entirely about adding and removing instances in a group and never mentions resizing one. The EC2 instance-type page states the key's cost directly: "you must stop your instance before you can change its instance type" and "plan for downtime while your instance is stopped", and resizing is described as moving between named instance types, which is what puts a ceiling at the largest one offered. No distractor is also correct: o2 proposes distributing a write path the stem says cannot be split; o3 proposes auto-scaling of instances for that same indivisible path, which the Auto Scaling page's launch-and-terminate model cannot serve; o4 proposes caching, which serves reads from a stored copy and cannot absorb writes. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A team resizes their single web server to the largest instance type their provider offers, hoping to both raise capacity and reduce outages. What has the resize achieved?

options.text: More capacity only. The server is still one machine and still a single point of failure, and it has now reached its ceiling with nowhere further to grow.
options.why: Vertical scaling does nothing for availability; a bigger single machine remains a single machine, and the largest instance type is a hard limit.

options.text: Both goals, since a larger instance type also comes with the provider's redundant power and network infrastructure built in — a belief that quietly assumes redundancy under the hypervisor is the same thing as redundancy at the level the application actually runs on.
options.why: Infrastructure redundancy underneath the instance does not make the instance itself redundant; the server is still a single point of failure at the application layer.

options.text: Neither goal, because the resize also required distributing the workload across multiple nodes first.
options.why: Vertical scaling by definition resizes one machine in place; it involves no distribution of the workload across nodes.

options.text: Reduced outages only, since larger instances fail less often than smaller ones.
options.why: Instance size is not what determines single-point-of-failure risk; a bigger machine is still exactly one machine that can go down.

items.rationale: Vertical scaling raises capacity up to the ceiling of the largest instance type offered, and it stops there — it does not remove the single point of failure a lone server represents, so an availability goal is left unaddressed.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation, for the same reason as vertical-scaling.01: the EC2 Auto Scaling page says nothing about resizing an instance. Repointed to the instance-type page, which describes the resize as changing one instance's type — one machine before and after — with downtime while it is stopped, so capacity rises and the single point of failure remains. No distractor is also correct: o2 treats infrastructure redundancy beneath the instance as redundancy of the instance, which the resize page gives no basis for; o3 claims the resize required distributing the workload, which contradicts a procedure performed on one stopped instance; o4 claims larger instances fail less often, which no cited source states and which does not change the count of machines. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A retail site slows every weekday at 09:00 and sits idle overnight. The current fix each quarter is to move the web server to a larger instance type; sessions live on local disk. Which single change addresses both the capacity ceiling and the site's single point of failure, and what has to be true of the application first?

options.text: Horizontal scaling — identical instances behind a load balancer — but only once sessions are moved off local disk, since a stateless design is the precondition for any instance serving any request.
options.why: Horizontal scaling removes the ceiling and the single point of failure, but it depends on statelessness; sessions pinned to one disk block any other instance from serving that user.

options.text: Vertical scaling to the next instance size, since a bigger machine removes both the ceiling and the single point of failure at once — an assumption that ignores both the restart the resize needs and the ceiling it will eventually hit, however large the next size is.
options.why: Vertical scaling still stops at the largest instance type and leaves one machine as the single point of failure; it solves neither problem the scenario names.

options.text: Horizontal scaling, and nothing about the application needs to change first, since a load balancer alone makes any backend interchangeable.
options.why: A load balancer distributes requests, but if sessions live on local disk, a request routed to a different instance still cannot find its own session — that gap is what stateless design closes.

options.text: Auto-scaling on a schedule, since the slow period is predictable and no design change is needed beyond a scaling policy.
options.why: A scheduled scaling policy still adds instances that are only useful once the workload is distributable; the sticky-session problem underneath is unaddressed.

items.rationale: Horizontal scaling is effectively unbounded and removes the single point of failure a lone server represents, but it only works if any instance can serve any request — which requires externalising session state first. Vertical scaling solves neither problem the scenario names; it just delays the ceiling.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the statelessness precondition the key turns on is absent from the EC2 Auto Scaling page. REL11-BP03 states it — "a best practice is to make services stateless where possible. This prevents loss of data or availability on resource restart", and Auto Scaling "can perform self-healing on stateless applications and add or remove capacity" — so sessions on local disk block the move, which is the key. The Auto Scaling page still supports the capacity half. No distractor is also correct: o2 claims a bigger instance removes both the ceiling and the single point of failure, and the instance-type page shows the resize leaves one stopped-then-restarted machine; o3 says nothing must change first, which BP03 contradicts; o4 offers a scheduled policy while leaving the local-disk sessions in place. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A batch job processes one large file start to finish on a single thread; nothing about the work can be split across machines. A team proposes adding ten more instances behind a load balancer to speed it up. What happens?

options.text: Nothing measurable; the extra instances sit idle, because the job's constraint is a single non-divisible thread of work that a load balancer cannot spread.
options.why: Horizontal scaling only helps work that can actually be divided; a load balancer has no requests to distribute across a single indivisible job.

options.text: The job finishes proportionally faster, since more instances behind a load balancer always raises throughput regardless of what the work looks like.
options.why: Throughput rises only when the added capacity can take on part of the work; assuming more instances always help ignores that this job has nothing to divide.

options.text: The job becomes highly available, since ten instances remove any single point of failure in the pipeline.
options.why: Surviving the loss of an idle instance is not the concern here; the job still runs to completion on whichever single thread is doing the work.

options.text: The job becomes elastic, since instances were added automatically in response to the workload.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario describes automatic, bidirectional capacity changes against demand; ten instances were simply added by a team's proposal.

items.rationale: Horizontal scaling only helps a workload that can actually be divided among instances. Putting more machines behind a load balancer does nothing for a single-threaded batch job with no distributable work, which is exactly the trap the exam sets with this shape of scenario.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item turns on a load balancer having nothing to distribute, which the EC2 Auto Scaling page does not address. The ELB overview states that a load balancer "distributes your incoming traffic across multiple targets" and routes requests only to healthy ones — it acts on requests, so a single indivisible job gives it nothing to spread, which is the key. No distractor is also correct: o2 asserts throughput always rises with instances, which the request-distribution model refutes for work that is not requests; o3 claims high availability, which is not what the stem measures and does not speed the single thread; o4 calls the manual proposal elastic, and neither the Auto Scaling page's policy-driven model nor NIST's rapid elasticity covers ten instances added by hand. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A scaling group is configured with a minimum of 2, a desired capacity of 4, and a maximum of 10. What do the minimum and maximum represent?

options.text: Guardrails the group's size may never cross — it will not be allowed to fall below 2 or rise above 10, whatever a policy or metric requests.
options.why: Minimum and maximum are hard bounds; they are not the target the group actively aims for.

options.text: Targets the group aims to reach as quickly as possible, ahead of the desired capacity — a reading that quietly promotes the number the group is actively held at into a number it is racing toward as fast as possible.
options.why: Desired capacity is the target the group is actively held at; minimum and maximum only bound how far policies are allowed to move it.

options.text: The number of healthy and unhealthy instances currently in the group.
options.why: Health status is a separate, continuously monitored property of each instance, not what these two configured numbers record.

options.text: The recovery point and recovery time the group is designed to meet.
options.why: Recovery objectives describe tolerable data loss and outage duration in disaster recovery, not capacity bounds on a scaling group.

items.rationale: A scaling group's minimum and maximum are guardrails the group's size may never cross, while desired capacity is the target the group is actively held at within those bounds — the maximum in particular exists to stop a runaway metric launching capacity without limit.

verification.reasoning: Key holds verbatim against the EC2 Auto Scaling page: "you can specify the minimum number of instances in each Auto Scaling group, and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling ensures that your group never goes below this size... the maximum number... never goes above this size. If you specify the desired capacity... ensures that your group has this many instances", and scaling policies "adjust the number of instances, within your minimum and maximum number of instances". Guardrails versus the actively held target is exactly the source's structure. No distractor is also correct: o2 makes minimum and maximum the target, which the page assigns to desired capacity; o3 confuses them with health status, which the page treats as a separate monitored property; o4 substitutes recovery objectives, which appear nowhere in the page's capacity model. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: An instance in a scaling group terminates unexpectedly, outside of any scale-in event. What does the scaling group do?

options.text: It launches a replacement to hold the group back at its desired capacity, without anyone being paged.
options.why: Documented health-based replacement means an unexpectedly terminated or impaired instance is replaced automatically to maintain desired capacity.

options.text: Nothing, until a human confirms the loss and manually requests a replacement instance.
options.why: Health-based replacement is automatic by design; the whole point is that an instance failure is repaired without a person being paged.

options.text: It raises the group's configured maximum capacity to compensate for the loss.
options.why: The configured maximum is a guardrail set deliberately; an unexpected termination does not change it, only the count of running instances within it.

options.text: It triggers a DNS-based redirection to a standby group in another region.
options.why: That describes a cross-site mechanism; a scaling group's own response to a lost member is to replace it within the same group, not to redirect elsewhere.

items.rationale: An auto-scaling group is also an availability mechanism: it monitors member health and replaces any instance found unhealthy or terminated unexpectedly, holding the group's desired capacity without human intervention.

verification.reasoning: Key holds verbatim against the EC2 Auto Scaling page: it "automatically monitors the health and availability of your instances using EC2 health checks and replaces terminated or impaired instances to maintain your desired capacity", and a custom health-check failure means the instance "is automatically replaced to maintain your desired capacity" — replacement to desired capacity with no human step. No distractor is also correct: o2 requires human confirmation, which the word "automatically" denies; o3 has the group raise its configured maximum, which the page describes as a bound the user sets; o4 describes a cross-region DNS redirection, which is nowhere in the group's documented response. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: An application keeps session data in the memory of whichever instance first served a user, and a load balancer is configured with sticky sessions to route each user back to that same instance every time. What does the sticky-session configuration reveal about the application?

options.text: That the application is not stateless; sticky sessions exist specifically to route a client back to the one instance holding its state.
options.why: Sticky sessions are the workaround for an application that has not externalised its session state, and their presence is the visible sign of that gap.

options.text: That the application is highly available, since every user's requests are reliably routed to a working instance.
options.why: Pinning a user to one instance is the opposite of resilience to that instance's loss; the pinned client's session dies along with its backend.

options.text: That the load balancer is performing failover, since routing based on a health signal is what failover means.
options.why: Sticky routing happens on every request from a given user, not only when an instance fails — that continuous behaviour is load balancing, not the failure-triggered switch failover names.

options.text: That the instance pool needs vertical scaling before it can serve more users.
options.why: Instance sizing is unrelated to whether requests can be freely routed among instances; the constraint here is where session state lives, not how big any one instance is.

items.rationale: Sticky sessions pin a client to the backend holding its state, which is the standard workaround for an application that is not stateless. Their presence is the tell: a truly stateless design would let the balancer route any request to any instance.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against the sticky-sessions page, which states a load balancer "routes each request independently to the registered instance with the smallest load" by default and that the sticky session feature "enables the load balancer to bind a user's session to a specific instance... all requests from the user during the session are sent to the same instance" — the configuration exists precisely because the instance holds the session, which REL11-BP03 identifies as the state that a stateless design would externalise. No distractor is also correct: o2 calls pinning highly available, and binding a session to one instance is what the stateless best practice warns loses availability on restart; o3 calls it failover, but the source describes stickiness acting on every request in the session, not on a failure; o4 raises instance sizing, which the source never ties to routing freedom. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A load balancer forwards TCP connections to backends without ever inspecting the request inside them, and a separate load balancer routes requests to different backend pools depending on the URL path. What is the difference between the two?

options.text: The first operates at the transport layer; the second operates at the application layer, where routing on path, hostname or header becomes possible.
options.why: Layer 4 forwards connections without inspecting them; layer 7 reads application-layer content such as the path to make its routing decision.

options.text: The first is failover and the second is load balancing, since only the second reacts to every request — a labelling error that assigns the failure-triggered name to two mechanisms that are both, in fact, acting on every single request.
options.why: Both examples described are load balancers acting on every request; failover is the separate, failure-triggered mechanism neither example describes.

options.text: The first is for internal traffic only, and the second is for traffic arriving from the public internet.
options.why: Nothing about layer 4 versus layer 7 routing determines whether traffic originates internally or externally; both can serve either source.

options.text: The first requires sticky sessions on every backend, and the second never needs them.
options.why: Sticky sessions are a workaround for stateful applications and apply independently of which layer the balancer operates at.

items.rationale: Balancers operate either at the transport layer, forwarding connections without inspecting them, or at the application layer, where content such as hostname, path or header can drive the routing decision — the two examples in the stem are exactly that pair.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the ELB overview page it cited never names an OSI layer. The two product pages state the key verbatim — an Application Load Balancer "functions at the application layer, the seventh layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model" and can "route requests to different target groups based on the content of the application traffic", while a Network Load Balancer "functions at the fourth layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model" and forwards to a target using the specified protocol and port. No distractor is also correct: o2 labels one of them failover, and both pages describe per-request routing; o3 ties the layers to internal versus internet traffic, which neither page does; o4 ties stickiness to layer, and the sticky-sessions page presents it as an optional feature independent of the OSI layer. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: An application externalises its session data to a shared cache and stores uploaded files in object storage instead of on local disk. Does this make the application stateless, meaning it stores no data at all?

options.text: Stateless describes where the state lives, not whether the system has any, so no; the application still has state, just not pinned to one server.
options.why: Externalising state is what makes instances interchangeable; it does not mean the state has been eliminated.

options.text: Yes — a stateless application by definition has no persistent data anywhere in the system — the specific misreading the concept exists to correct, that no state anywhere is the same claim as no state pinned to one server.
options.why: This is the specific misreading the concept guards against: statelessness is about the locality of state, not its absence.

options.text: No, because moving data to a shared cache makes the application highly available instead.
options.why: A dependency on the shared store's own availability is a real consequence of this design, but it is not the reason the 'no data at all' reading is wrong.

options.text: Yes, but only once the application is also placed behind a load balancer.
options.why: Statelessness is a property of where the application keeps its data, decided in the code; a load balancer's presence or absence does not change that.

items.rationale: Statelessness means no client-specific state is pinned to a particular server between requests. The data still exists — in a shared cache, a database, or object storage — the design choice is only about where it is not stored: locally.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL11-BP03, which recommends making services stateless "where possible" so that "loss of data or availability on resource restart" is prevented, and recommends replacing the entire resource — a recommendation that is only coherent if the state still exists somewhere off the resource. Statelessness is therefore about where state lives, not whether the system has any. No distractor is also correct: o2's "no persistent data anywhere" would make the best practice unimplementable for any real workload; o3 substitutes high availability for the reason the reading is wrong; o4 makes a load balancer's presence decide the property, which the best practice locates in how the service is built. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: An auto-scaling policy terminates an instance mid-shift to bring the group back down to its desired capacity. Which property of the application determines whether any user notices?

options.text: Whether the application is stateless — an interchangeable instance can be terminated and replaced without anyone's session or in-flight work being tied to it specifically.
options.why: Statelessness is the precondition that lets auto-scaling, load balancing and instance replacement all happen without a user-visible fault.

options.text: Whether the group's configured maximum capacity is set high enough to absorb the loss.
options.why: The maximum bounds how large the group may grow; it says nothing about whether a terminated instance was holding state a user depended on.

options.text: Whether the instance being terminated was the primary in an active-passive pair.
options.why: Active-passive versus active-active describes how redundant capacity is deployed, not whether any one instance held irreplaceable client state.

options.text: Whether the termination also triggers a scale-out event on a standby instance pool in another region — describing a cross-region event that nothing in the scenario supports, when the change described is a routine single-pool scale-in.
options.why: A routine scale-in within one pool of interchangeable instances is not a cross-region event; it only becomes user-visible if the application is not stateless.

items.rationale: Stateless design is what makes instance termination safe: because no request depends on reaching the same instance twice, an auto-scaling group can remove an instance mid-shift and the load balancer simply routes the next request to a survivor, with nothing user-visible lost.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-reliability-pillar, whose page is the Reliability Pillar welcome page and contains only an abstract, the list of six pillars and a statement of the paper's audience — none of the content this item turns on. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against REL11-BP03 read with the EC2 Auto Scaling page: stateless services prevent "loss of data or availability on resource restart", and Auto Scaling "can perform self-healing on stateless applications and add or remove capacity" — so whether a scale-in is user-visible turns on statelessness. No distractor is also correct: o2 offers the configured maximum, which the Auto Scaling page defines as an upper bound on group size and not a property of any instance's state; o3 offers active-passive placement, which describes how redundant capacity is deployed; o4 invents a cross-region scale-out that neither source attaches to a single-group scale-in. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A dashboard reports average response time as healthy, but users are complaining about slow page loads. What is the average likely hiding, and what should be reported instead?

options.text: A slow tail of requests; a percentile such as p95 or p99 should be reported instead, since an average conceals the worst-performing minority.
options.why: Latency is a distribution, not a single number; percentiles surface the slow requests that an average smooths away.

options.text: Low throughput — requests per second should be reported instead of a time-based measurement.
options.why: Throughput is a different quantity entirely, measuring volume rather than delay, and would not explain a complaint specifically about per-request slowness.

options.text: A bandwidth shortfall — the link's raw capacity should be reported instead of application response time.
options.why: Bandwidth is the capacity of the link, not what the system actually achieves over it, and neither is what a per-request latency complaint is measuring.

options.text: Nothing — average response time is definitionally equal to the experience of a typical user.
options.why: An average is skewed by the whole distribution and can look healthy even while a meaningful minority of users are timing out.

items.rationale: Latency is reported as a distribution because an average hides the slow tail. Percentiles such as p95 or p99 are quoted precisely because the worst few percent of requests are what users notice and complain about.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-pillars, whose entire page is the building analogy plus a bulleted list of the six pillar names — it contains nothing about this item's subject. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds against SRE Chapter 6, which warns against designing on the mean and gives the arithmetic: "if you run a web service with an average latency of 100 ms at 1,000 requests per second, 1% of requests might easily take 5 seconds", adding that "the 99th percentile of one backend can easily become the median response of your frontend" and recommending latency histograms to separate a slow average from a slow tail. No distractor is also correct: o2 substitutes throughput, a volume measure the same chapter lists separately as traffic; o3 substitutes link bandwidth; o4 asserts the average equals the typical experience, which the chapter's own example disproves. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A queue processor starts batching many small write operations into one larger write to raise throughput. What is the predictable cost?

options.text: Higher latency for every item now waiting for its batch to fill before being written.
options.why: Batching trades per-item delay for aggregate volume; each item waits longer so the batch it belongs to can complete.

options.text: Lower throughput, since batching adds processing overhead that outweighs any gain.
options.why: Batching is chosen specifically because it raises throughput by amortising per-operation overhead across many items, not because it lowers it.

options.text: No cost, since latency and throughput are two names for the same underlying measurement.
options.why: The two use different units and are not derivable from one another; a system can be excellent at one while poor at the other, exactly as here.

options.text: Reduced availability, since batched writes are more likely to fail outright.
options.why: Nothing about grouping writes together changes whether the underlying storage is redundant or fault tolerant; the trade being made is purely delay versus volume.

items.rationale: Optimising one of latency or throughput can actively worsen the other. Batching many small operations into one larger one raises throughput and simultaneously raises the latency of every item now waiting for the batch to fill — the exam's standard example of the trade-off.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the item cited aws-well-architected-pillars, whose entire page is the building analogy plus a bulleted list of the six pillar names — it contains nothing about this item's subject. Citation repointed and re-verified. Key holds: the Kinesis Producer Library page documents the throughput half directly — aggregation stores multiple records in one stream record and "allows customers to increase the number of records sent per API call, which effectively increases producer throughput", with the worked example of packing 1,000 records into 10 — and the per-item wait is entailed by that mechanism, since a record cannot be sent until the batch it is packed into is assembled, against Chapter 6's treatment of latency as per-request delay. Noted in qbank-findings: the delay half is entailed rather than stated, which is the thinnest sourcing left in this file. No distractor is also correct: o2 says batching lowers throughput, which the KPL page contradicts; o3 equates latency and throughput, which Chapter 6 separates as distinct golden signals; o4 claims batched writes are likelier to fail outright, which no source states and which grouping does not affect. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A team stores frequently-read database query results in an in-process memory cache to cut repeated work. A separate team serves their site's static images from edge locations distributed around the world, close to each viewer. Which of the two is a content delivery network, and what makes it a distinct case of the same underlying technique?

options.text: The second — a CDN is caching plus geography: it is one specific deployment of the general technique, distinguished by its edge locations sitting near the viewer rather than in application memory.
options.why: Every CDN is a cache, but not every cache is a CDN; the CDN's distinguishing property is geographic distribution, not the caching mechanism itself.

options.text: Both equally, since an in-process cache and a set of edge locations are simply two names for one identical mechanism — collapsing the general technique and its geographically distributed special case into a single mechanism with no distinguishing property left.
options.why: They are the same general technique at different scope: the CDN adds geographic distribution on top of the caching behaviour the in-process cache already has.

options.text: The first, because a CDN specifically avoids storing any data and only forwards requests toward the nearest origin.
options.why: Forwarding without storing describes routing, not caching; a CDN's edge locations do store copies, which is what lets them serve a fresh request without contacting the origin.

options.text: Neither, since caching and content delivery are unrelated techniques that happen to share the word 'edge'.
options.why: A CDN is explicitly a deployment of caching, not an unrelated technique; the exam expects the general form to be recognised inside its specific deployments.

items.rationale: Caching is the general technique — a key, a value and an expiry, usable at any layer. A CDN is caching applied with geographic distribution: edge locations near each viewer, holding a copy of what the origin serves. Every CDN is a cache; not every cache is a CDN.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against the CloudFront introduction, which describes delivery "through a worldwide network of data centers called edge locations", each request "routed to the edge location that provides the lowest latency", with copies "held (or cached) in multiple edge locations around the world" — a CDN is caching distinguished by geography, so the second team's setup is the CDN and the in-process cache is the general technique. No distractor is also correct: o2 collapses the two into one mechanism, erasing the geographic distinction the page draws; o3 claims a CDN stores nothing, contradicted by "if the content is already in the edge location... CloudFront delivers it immediately"; o4 calls them unrelated techniques, contradicted by the page's own caching language. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A cached product page is served to every visitor for an hour before its entry expires, even though the price changed twenty minutes ago. What trade did the cache make, and what does it not remove the need for?

options.text: Staleness, in exchange for lower latency and origin load — and it does not remove the need for an origin capable of serving the full load, since a cold start or invalidation still sends requests there.
options.why: The cost of caching is always the possibility of serving something stale, and the cache is non-authoritative — the origin must still be able to survive real load.

options.text: Nothing — a correctly configured cache never serves data more than a few seconds old — an assumption that quietly rules out the entire mechanism time-to-live exists to permit, which is exactly what makes caching cheap.
options.why: Staleness up to the full time-to-live is exactly what a cache can serve; describing it as never happening ignores the trade the technique makes by design.

options.text: Latency, in exchange for guaranteed data freshness on every single request.
options.why: This reverses the actual trade: caching improves latency at the cost of possible staleness, not the other way round.

options.text: Availability, since a cache miss makes the requested page temporarily unreachable until the origin responds.
options.why: A cache miss still serves the request by falling through to the origin; it does not make the page unreachable, only slower for that one request.

items.rationale: Caching cuts latency and origin load at the cost of possibly serving a stale value until expiry, invalidation or eviction. Because a cached copy is not authoritative, the origin still has to be capable of handling the full load on a cold start or after invalidation.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on the citation: the staleness-until-expiry mechanism the item turns on is absent from the CloudFront introduction. The expiration page states it — CloudFront "serves a file from an edge location until the cache duration that you specified passes — that is, until the file expires", after which the next request is forwarded to the origin to check for a newer version, and a rarely requested file "might" be evicted early — and the introduction supplies the non-authoritative part: the origin "stores the original, definitive version of your objects". Together they give the key: staleness traded for latency and origin load, with the origin still required. No distractor is also correct: o2 denies staleness beyond a few seconds, contradicted by a configurable duration whose default TTL is 24 hours; o3 reverses the trade; o4 claims a miss makes the page unreachable, contradicted by the documented fall-through to the origin. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: Users in a distant region report slow page loads for a media-heavy site while users near the origin report no problem at all. Separately, every user everywhere reports a specific search feature is slow, including users sitting next to the origin. Which symptom is a CDN, such as Amazon CloudFront, the right fix for, and why does it not help the other?

options.text: The first — a CDN removes geographic distance for the regional symptom; the second is universal, which points at the origin, a query, or another bottleneck that edge caching cannot change.
options.why: A CDN answers a distance problem specifically; a slowdown that is uniform everywhere, including at the origin, is not a distance problem.

options.text: The second — a CDN accelerates any slow request regardless of cause, including database queries, once content is placed at the edge — extending the edge’s reach to a class of request it was never built to accelerate, since a query’s own execution time never touches the network at all.
options.why: A CDN serves cacheable content from the edge; a search query's own execution time on the origin is unaffected by where static content is cached.

options.text: Both equally, since adding edge locations always reduces total request time for every user.
options.why: The universal symptom is present even next to the origin, which is exactly what a distance problem does not look like — the fix has to be elsewhere.

options.text: Neither — a CDN only ever serves images and video, so a general page-load complaint is out of scope for it entirely.
options.why: A CDN typically serves static objects, which does include page assets like images, so the regional symptom described is a standard case for one.

items.rationale: The symptom that identifies a CDN is specific: distant users slow, nearby users fine — a distance problem no amount of origin capacity fixes. A universal slowdown present even beside the origin is not a distance problem, so an edge cache changes nothing about it.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against the CloudFront introduction: requests are routed "to the edge location that provides the lowest latency", the AWS backbone "dramatically reduces the number of networks that your users' requests must pass through", and what is served from the edge is the content copied from the origin — all of which addresses distance, and none of which touches work executed on the origin. A slowdown present beside the origin is therefore not the case a CDN answers. No distractor is also correct: o2 claims the edge accelerates any request including database queries, which the page's copy-at-the-edge model does not do; o3 claims every user gets a reduction, contradicted by the universal symptom in the stem; o4 claims a CDN serves only images and video, contradicted by the page's list of .html, .css, .js and image files, plus dynamic content. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A CDN's edge server receives a request for an object it has never cached before. What has to happen before that first viewer at that edge gets a response?

options.text: The edge must fetch the object from the origin, the definitive copy, before it can return anything, and it keeps a copy afterward for later requests.
options.why: A CDN does not make the origin faster and does not help the very first request to a given edge, which must be satisfied from the origin.

options.text: Nothing extra — every edge location shares one global cache, so a miss at one edge is always a hit at another — an assumption that erases the whole reason edges are described as geographically distributed rather than as one shared pool.
options.why: Edge locations are geographically distributed caches; a miss at one is not automatically covered by another edge holding a copy.

options.text: The edge must invalidate every other edge's copy of the same object first.
options.why: Invalidation removes an object before its time-to-live expires when content changes; it has no role in serving a first, uncached request.

options.text: The origin must first push the object out to every edge location in the network.
options.why: A CDN is typically pull-based: edges fetch on demand from the origin and retain a copy, rather than the origin proactively pushing to every location.

items.rationale: The origin holds the original, definitive copy. A viewer's request resolving to a nearby edge that has never seen the object still requires a fetch from the origin before anything can be returned; only subsequent requests to that edge are served from its cache.

Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A dashboard alerts when CPU utilisation crosses a threshold someone configured last quarter. A separate practice lets an engineer, faced with an unfamiliar failure nobody predicted, reconstruct what happened by correlating logs, metrics and traces. Which of the two is monitoring, and what can it not do that the other can?

options.text: The first is monitoring — it answers a question chosen in advance; it cannot answer a question nobody thought to ask, which is what the second practice, observability, is built for.
options.why: Monitoring requires the threshold to be known before the event; observability is the property that lets an unanticipated question be answered from logs, metrics and traces together.

options.text: The second is monitoring, since correlating multiple signal types is simply a more advanced form of threshold alerting — reversing which practice requires the question to be known in advance and which one exists precisely because it cannot always be.
options.why: This swaps the pair: threshold alerting on a predefined signal is monitoring, and combining logs, metrics and traces to answer an unanticipated question is observability instead.

options.text: Both are the same practice under different names, since both ultimately rely on numeric time-series data.
options.why: Observability draws on logs and traces as well as metrics, and its defining feature — answering unanticipated questions — is not something monitoring's predefined thresholds provide.

options.text: Neither, because both are simply names for a dashboard, and any dashboard showing logs beside metrics already delivers everything either practice offers.
options.why: A dashboard is a display surface for whichever signals were collected; it does not decide whether an unanticipated question can be answered, which is what separates the two practices.

items.rationale: Monitoring collects predefined numeric signals and alerts when a chosen threshold is crossed — it answers questions you knew to ask in advance. Observability is the broader property, built from logs, metrics and traces together, that lets you answer questions you had not anticipated; metrics are one input to it, not a synonym for it.

items.stem: The golden signals framework names four metrics to watch first for a running API. Which four should be the starting point, and what does the fourth mean specifically?

options.text: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation, saturation meaning how full the constraining resource is, not merely how busy it appears.
options.why: These are the four signals Google's SRE material names first, and saturation is specifically about queued work against the tightest resource, distinct from simple utilisation.

options.text: CPU, memory, disk and network, since those are the only resources that can ever be the constraint.
options.why: The golden signals are user-facing service signals, not a fixed list of hardware resources, and the actual constraint can also be an external dependency.

options.text: Uptime, cost, latency and throughput, since those are the numbers customers care about most.
options.why: Cost is a separate business concern the golden-signals framework does not include, and the correct fourth signal is saturation, not throughput.

options.text: Errors, latency, availability and elasticity, since those cover both failure and demand-tracking behaviour.
options.why: Elasticity is a design property, not a metric to alert a threshold on, and this list omits traffic and saturation entirely.

items.rationale: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Saturation specifically measures how full the constraining resource is — queued work against it — which is what actually drives user-visible latency as a system approaches its limit.

SRE Chapter 6 states the key verbatim: "the four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. If you can only measure four metrics of your user-facing system, focus on these four", and treats saturation as how full the service is against its most constrained resource, noting that "measuring your 99th percentile response time... can give a very early signal of saturation".
