Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A team measures the fraction of successful requests as its SLI, and holds an internal target of 99.95% against that measurement — tighter than the 99.9% figure with service credits it publishes to customers. Which term names the internal target, and how does it differ from the customer-facing figure?

options.text: The SLO, an internal target set on the SLI, distinct from the SLA because missing it carries no contractual consequence on its own.
options.why: An SLO is a target value on a measurement; only the SLA, the separate contract with users, attaches an explicit remedy to a missed number.

options.text: The SLA, since it is the number the organisation is actually held to internally on a day-to-day basis.
options.why: The SLA is specifically the external contract with users and their remedy; the tighter, internally-held number here is the SLO, held deliberately stricter as a safety margin.

options.text: The SLI, because 99.95% is itself a direct measurement of request success rather than a target.
options.why: 99.95% here is described as a target set on the measurement, not the measurement itself; the SLI is the fraction of successful requests being measured against it.

options.text: There is no internal target distinct from the customer figure, since a provider only ever tracks the number it publishes.
options.why: Holding an internal target tighter than the externally published figure is standard practice specifically so there is room to act before a contractual consequence is triggered.

items.rationale: The SLI is the measurement, the SLO is the internal target set on that measurement, and the SLA is the contract with users that attaches consequences to meeting or missing it. Holding the SLO tighter than the SLA, as here, is the standard safety-margin practice.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against SRE Chapter 4, which defines an SLI as "a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided", an SLO as "a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI", and an SLA as "an explicit or implicit contract with your users that includes consequences of meeting (or missing) the SLOs they contain" — adding that the distinction is drawn by whether consequences attach, and that internal targets are commonly held tighter than what is promised externally. No distractor is also correct: o2 names the SLA for an internally held target with no remedy; o3 calls the target the measurement; o4 denies that a distinct internal target exists, which the chapter's treatment of SLOs contradicts. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: A database server is at 40% CPU utilisation, but its disk queue is deep, with requests waiting well before they are served. Which resource is the bottleneck, and what distinguishes it from the CPU figure?

options.text: The disk; saturation, not utilisation, is what identifies the constraint, and the deep queue shows work is waiting on the disk specifically.
options.why: Utilisation says how busy a resource looks; saturation says how much work is queued waiting for it, and it is saturation that tracks the latency users feel.

options.text: The CPU, since 40% utilisation is already the highest reported number in the scenario.
options.why: A moderate utilisation figure with no queue behind it is not saturated; the constraint is wherever work is actually piling up, which is the disk here.

options.text: Neither — the bottleneck must be network, since that is the resource most often saturated in cloud deployments generally.
options.why: The scenario gives no network figures at all; the constraint has to be identified from the evidence given, which points at the disk queue.

options.text: Both equally, since CPU and disk always saturate together on any single server.
options.why: The two resources are independent; this scenario specifically shows one saturated (disk) and one merely busy (CPU), which is the point being tested.

items.rationale: Utilisation measures how much of a resource is in use; saturation measures how much work is queued waiting for it, and only the saturated resource is the actual constraint. A moderately busy CPU next to a deeply queued disk means the disk, not the CPU, is where the fix belongs.

items.stem: Support reports checkout feels slow. A team's first move is to add more application instances behind the load balancer, but p99 latency does not improve. What step was skipped?

options.text: Measuring which resource is actually saturated before acting — the fix should follow the identified constraint, not the most familiar-looking one.
options.why: Effort spent on any resource other than the one that is saturated changes nothing measurable; the constraint has to be found first.

options.text: Nothing was skipped, since adding instances is always the correct first response to any latency complaint — application capacity being the usual constraint behind a slow checkout, and the one lever a team can pull without waiting for a measurement.
options.why: Horizontal scaling helps only if application capacity was the actual constraint; if the real bottleneck sits elsewhere, such as a database's disk, added instances change nothing.

options.text: Setting a recovery time objective for the checkout service before making the change.
options.why: Recovery objectives describe disaster-recovery targets around restoring service after a major failure, not a live performance-tuning decision.

options.text: Placing a content delivery network in front of the checkout page.
options.why: A CDN helps a regional distance problem for cacheable content; it does not address a database-side constraint behind a dynamic checkout flow.

items.rationale: The ordering matters more than the technique: measure each resource under load, find the one that is actually saturated, and only then apply a fix aimed at it. Adding instances without first locating the constraint is exactly the attractive wrong answer the exam supplies.
